title: LR vs. SVM & the SGDClassifier
intro: The final score of the course: when do you choose logistic regression and when an SVM? And as a cherry on top: the SGDClassifier, which proves that these models differ only in their loss function.

blocks.html:
Both are linear classifiers, and both can work with kernels — though it is more common with SVMs, because predictions are much faster when the number of support vectors is small. Both can be talked into producing probabilities, but with logistic regression that is natural (it is built into the loss), while with SVMs it takes extra work. Both extend to multi-class via one-vs-rest or by adapting the loss directly.

The sharpest difference remains: with logistic regression (as with most methods) all data points influence the fit; with an SVM only the support vectors matter — the rest can go. And finally a matter of definition: "logistic regression" does not refer to a specific type of regularisation, but "SVM" by convention means: linear classifier with hinge loss plus L2 regularisation.

rows: common — fast with few support vectors

blocks.html: Fitting a linear SVM can also be done via SVC(kernel='linear'), but LinearSVC is often faster. And there are more hyperparameters than these — dare to read the documentation.

sections.title: SGDClassifier: proof that only the loss differs

blocks.html:
Finally, a class that illustrates the red thread of the course: SGDClassifier (SGD = stochastic gradient descent). It can handle much larger datasets than the other methods. The beautiful part: to switch between logistic regression and a linear SVM you only need to change the loss hyperparameter — the model is the same, only the loss changes. Exactly what we saw in chapter 2.

One "gotcha": the regularisation hyperparameter here is called alpha instead of C — and a larger alpha means more regularisation. In short: alpha is the inverse of C.

blocks.caption: Two lines to switch between LR and a linear SVM
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_tr)
X_tr, X_te = scaler.transform(X_tr), scaler.transform(X_te)

for loss, label in [('hinge', 'linear SVM'), ('log_loss', 'logistic regression')]:
    sgd = SGDClassifier(loss=loss, max_iter=2000, tol=1e-3, random_state=42)
    sgd.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f'loss={loss:<9} ({label})  train={sgd.score(X_tr, y_tr):.3f}'
          f'  test={sgd.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}')

blocks.html: Linear classifiers share one prediction step (the sign of \( w \cdot x + b \)); what distinguishes them is the loss optimised during fitting — logistic loss, hinge loss, or something else.

sections.title: Where does all of this fit in the bigger picture?

blocks.html:
Zoom out: data science is answering questions and making decisions based on data, and combines pieces such as data collection, data preparation, database design, visualisation, communication, software engineering and machine learning. Within machine learning there are branches like supervised learning, unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning; we stayed inside supervised learning — predicting a target from features with labelled data. Within supervised learning we focused on classification (categorical targets), and within that on the two most popular linear classifiers: logistic regression and SVMs.

A lot learned — and at the same time the tip of the iceberg. Next steps to explore: non-linear classifiers in depth, tree-based methods (random forests, boosting), or heading towards unsupervised learning.
